title: 3-Phase Brushless Motors, Pole Pairs and 90-Degree Electrical Torque Lead

blocks.x: Convert mechanical shaft angle $\theta_m$ into **electrical angle** $\theta_e = N_p \theta_m$ for a brushless motor with $N_p$ **pole pairs**, and compute the balanced 3-phase sinusoidal coil voltages $(v_a, v_b, v_c)$ that keep the stator magnetic field locked **$90^\circ$ electrical ahead** of the rotor magnets for smooth maximum torque.

blocks.x: Idea 1: Pole pairs ($N_p$) and electrical angle versus mechanical shaft angle ($\theta_e = N_p \cdot \theta_m$)

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Wikipedia — Brushless DC electric motor (" Construction" & "Variations")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brushless_DC_electric_motor) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Brushless DC electric motor`** and **`Implementations`**.
**What to skip:** Skip aircraft starter-generator history.

**Key takeaway:** Unlike a brushed DC motor whose mechanical brushes flip coil polarity automatically, a **3-phase brushless motor (`BLDC`)** has stationary copper coils (**stator**) and a rotating bell lined with permanent magnets (**rotor**). If the rotor has $14$ alternating North and South magnets, it has **$N_p = 7$ pole pairs**. Every time the physical shaft rotates by $\frac{1}{7}$ of a turn ($51.43^\circ$ mechanical), the magnetic pattern repeats a full $360^\circ$ **electrical angle**: $\theta_e = N_p \cdot \theta_m$.

**Alternative resource:** [MathsIsFun — Sine, Cosine and Tangent](https://www.mathsisfun.com/sine-cosine-tangent.html) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]` — Review how $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ repeat every $2\pi\text{ rad}$ ($360^\circ$).

blocks.x: Idea 2: 3-phase sinusoidal commutation and $90^\circ$ electrical torque lead

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Wikipedia — Three-phase electric power ("Principle")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-phase_electric_power) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`

**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Three-phase electric power`** and **`Principle`** (how three waveforms offset by $120^\circ = \frac{2\pi}{3}\text{ rad}$ create a smoothly rotating magnetic field).
**What to skip:** Skip high-voltage utility grid transformers.

**Key takeaway:** Imagine pulling a compass needle around a circle with a handheld magnet. If you hold your magnet directly on top of the needle ($0^\circ$ lead), the needle just pulls radially outward against its bearing with **zero turning torque**. To get maximum tangential pull, you must hold your stator magnetic field **$90^\circ$ electrical ($\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$) ahead** of the rotor's electrical angle $\theta_e$ ($\tau \propto \sin(\theta_{\text{stator}} - \theta_e) = \sin(90^\circ) = 1.0$) using three $120^\circ$-shifted phase voltages.

**Alternative resource:** [The Physics Classroom — Magnetic Field and the Right-Hand Rule](https://www.physicsclassroom.com/class/circuits/Lesson-2/What-is-an-Electric-Circuit) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]` — Review closed current loops in motor windings.

blocks.x: In a **3-phase brushless motor** with **$N_p$ pole pairs**, reading the mechanical shaft angle $\theta_m$ from your magnetic encoder (`Lesson 03.1`) immediately tells the microcontroller where the rotor magnets sit in **electrical angle**:

To produce smooth, ripple-free rotary torque (**sinusoidal commutation**, the foundation of `SimpleFOC` and **Brushless Motor Control Lab** of the MechaLab Workbench), we command a stator magnetic field angle $\theta_{\text{drive}} = \theta_e + \frac{\pi}{2}$ (**$90^\circ$ electrical torque lead**) across the three stator phases ($A, B, C$) spaced $120^\circ$ ($\frac{2\pi}{3}\text{ rad}$) apart:

blocks.tex: v_a = V_q \cos(\theta_{\text{drive}}), \qquad v_b = V_q \cos\!\left(\theta_{\text{drive}} - \frac{2\pi}{3}\right), \qquad v_c = V_q \cos\!\left(\theta_{\text{drive}} - \frac{4\pi}{3}\right)

blocks.x: Notice that at any angle $\theta_{\text{drive}}$, the three phase voltages remain balanced ($v_a + v_b + v_c = 0$), and because torque varies with $\sin(\Delta\theta_e)$, keeping $\Delta\theta_e = +90^\circ$ ($\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$) yields $100\%$ of the motor's available torque per Ampere whereas $\Delta\theta_e = 0^\circ$ yields $0\%$ torque and only wastes heat in the windings.

def three_phase_voltages(theta_e_rad, v_q):
    drive_rad = theta_e_rad + (math.pi / 2.0)
    va = v_q * math.cos(drive_rad)
    vb = v_q * math.cos(drive_rad - 2.0 * math.pi / 3.0)
    vc = v_q * math.cos(drive_rad - 4.0 * math.pi / 3.0)
    return va, vb, vc

import math


def mech_to_elec_deg(mech_deg, pole_pairs):
    elec_deg = (mech_deg * pole_pairs) % 360.0
    return elec_deg


def three_phase_voltages(theta_e_rad, v_q):
    drive_rad = theta_e_rad + (math.pi / 2.0)
    va = v_q * math.cos(drive_rad)
    vb = v_q * math.cos(drive_rad - 2.0 * math.pi / 3.0)
    vc = v_q * math.cos(drive_rad - 4.0 * math.pi / 3.0)
    return va, vb, vc


for m_deg in [0.0, 10.0, 25.7143]:
    e_deg = mech_to_elec_deg(m_deg, pole_pairs=7)
    print(f"Mech={m_deg:7.4f} deg (Np=7) -> Elec={e_deg:5.1f} deg")

va, vb, vc = three_phase_voltages(theta_e_rad=0.0, v_q=6.0)
print(f"At theta_e=0.0 rad (vq=6.0 V): va={va:+.2f} V, vb={vb:+.2f} V, vc={vc:+.2f} V (sum={va+vb+vc:+.2f} V)")

items.x: **Confusing total magnet poles ($14$) with pole pairs ($N_p = 7$):** Datasheets often label a motor `12N14P` ($12$ stator slots, $14$ rotor magnet poles). Always divide the magnet pole count by $2$ to get $N_p = 7$ pole pairs before multiplying $\theta_e = N_p \theta_m$.

**Applying voltage-mode commutation (`vq = 6 V`) to a low-resistance drone motor ($R = 0.05\ \Omega$):** Without current sensors, stalling a $0.05\ \Omega$ motor at $6\text{ V}$ draws $I = 6 / 0.05 = 120\text{ A}$! Only use open-loop/voltage-mode `SimpleFOC` on high-resistance gimbal motors ($R \approx 8\text{–}15\ \Omega$, where $I_{\text{stall}} \approx 0.6\text{ A}$).

**Pole pairs to electrical angle:** A gimbal brushless motor has $22$ permanent magnets around its rotor bell ($N_p = 11$ pole pairs). When the mechanical shaft rotates by $15^\circ$, how many electrical degrees does the magnetic field advance? Answer
**Why $0^\circ$ electrical lead fails:** What happens if the stator magnetic field points at $\Delta\theta_e = 0^\circ$ (directly aligned with the rotor magnet) instead of $+90^\circ$ ahead? Answer

blocks.x: It produces **zero rotary torque** ($\sin 0^\circ = 0$)! All coil current goes into pulling radially on the rotor bearings and heating the copper windings.

items.x: A brushless rotor with $2 N_p$ magnets has **$N_p$ pole pairs**, advancing through **electrical angle** $\theta_e = N_p \theta_m$.
**3-phase sinusoidal commutation** drives three $120^\circ$-spaced coils with $\theta_{\text{drive}} = \theta_e + \frac{\pi}{2}$ (**$90^\circ$ electrical torque lead**) for smooth maximum torque.
